brief.notification_title: AI stocks rebound, but Fed hike bets lift the dollar
brief.market_summary: Prices are intraday at 12:13 ET Wednesday, so there are no closes yet. AI stocks are bouncing hard after CoreWeave's beat-and-raise: Nasdaq +2.03%, SMH +6.23%, S&P 500 +1.38% to 7,625. The Dow is only +0.19%, and defensive sectors are lower. The rate backdrop got worse, not better. Futures put about 90% odds on a December hike, Waller is openly discussing 50bp, and the dollar index is at a 19-month high of 102.91. The 10-year sits near 4.998%, but the cash Treasury market is closed for Veterans Day, so treat that level as indicative. Brent is up 2.3% to $93.62 because Iran denied any talks, even though Saudi output surged 26%. Crypto is bouncing less than tech (BTC $74,153, +1.6%) and is still down sharply on the week as ETF outflows continue.
brief.since_last: Hot October CPI (+0.4% headline, +0.3% core) was already in yesterday's brief. Three things are new. (1) AI stocks reversed higher. CoreWeave reported revenue of $3.66B against $3.55B expected, raised its 2026 guide to $13.0–13.3B, and its CEO cancelled his planned share sales (n36). That lifted chips broadly (n45, n50), and NVDA was +4% at 11:00 ET despite a downgrade (n78). (2) The Fed got more hawkish in public. Goolsbee called the CPI report "borderline disturbing" (n11), Waller said 50bp should be considered, Logan wants two more hikes, Goldman and UBS now expect hikes in December and March (n107), and the dollar hit a 19-month high (n13). (3) Oil now has two opposing supply stories. Saudi Arabia told OPEC it pumped 10.563M bpd in October, up 26% and back near pre-war levels (n48), and total OPEC output rose about 2M bpd (n123). Against that, Iran denied it is in talks, ship attacks continue, and a drone hit Russia's Ust-Luga export hub (n12, n117). Data caveats: the cash bond market is closed today, the calendar lists a 10-year auction at 5.020% that my research could not confirm, and I have no Brent settlement.

economic_data.takeaway: This was the third straight brisk monthly rise (n162). There is no y/y figure because October 2025 prices were not collected. It is the main reason futures price about 90% odds of a December hike and the 2-year jumped 17bp on the official curve.

This is the level Waller said would justify considering 50bp. Core has been 0.3% or higher in 5 of 10 months this year, which supports the dollar and the front end of the curve and works against long-duration assets.
Expectations are stuck near 4%, so the Fed has little room to look through the CPI print.
Growth is strong and inflation is hot, the mix that argues for more hikes. Nothing here suggests the economy needs relief.
Flat. It doesn't move markets, but it fits the CNBC/NRF report of consumers showing strain (n148).
A large build that traders ignored as Iran headlines dominated. When bearish inventory data gets shrugged off, the geopolitical premium is still in charge of price.
About 30bp lower than last month's yield, which shows how far yields fell in October. No consensus was given to judge demand.
Treat this with caution. The cash market is closed for Veterans Day and my research found no 10-year result. If it is real, it cleared above 5%, near my IEF limit.
Claims are low and the labour market is tight. Only a jump well above 200K would start to argue against a 50bp hike.
Pipeline inflation. The forecasts already assume a big drop from September's 1.3%, so the risk is a smaller drop than expected.
Core PPI at 0.5% or higher would push 50bp odds up and the 10-year above 5%, and it triggers my rule to cancel the unfilled IEF tranche. A 0.2–0.3% print lets yields settle.

earnings.result: EPS -$1.28 vs -$1.45 est. Revenue $3.66B (+168%) vs $3.55B consensus and above its own $3.45–3.60B guide. 2026 revenue guide raised to $13.0–13.3B vs $12.86B consensus. Backlog $132.5B. Net loss $709M. CEO cancelled his share-sale plan.
earnings.takeaway: The stock is up 20–23%. This is the catalyst for the whole AI rebound (n45, n50): it eased fears that AI spending is being cut. It is still a heavily leveraged buyer of chips, so it tells you about demand, not about the margins of chipmakers or equipment makers.
A clean beat in aerospace aftermarket. It supports XLI (+1.3% today, +0.9% on the week) as one of the few cyclical groups holding up while yields rise.
Oil producers are still very profitable at $90+ Brent. Compare Ecopetrol below: operations matter more than the oil price.

The LNG exporter benefits from wartime gas tightness and demand for backup power (n5). The read-through to Brent is limited.

sections.summary: The rebound is real but narrow. It is driven by AI and chip stocks after CoreWeave reduced fears about AI spending. XLK is +4.07% and SMH +6.23%, while the Dow (+0.19%), health care (-0.77%) and staples (-0.52%) are lagging. The index rose despite worse rate news, which makes it fragile. The Nasdaq is still -6% over a month and SMH -12.6%.
key_points: S&P 500 7,625 (+1.38%) and Nasdaq 25,574 (+2.03%) after Tuesday's -0.38% / -0.74%. VIX 17.80 (-8.5%) but still +16.6% over a month.
CoreWeave +20–23% on a revenue beat and guide raise. NBIS +17% and NVDA +4% even after a downgrade (n78) and scrutiny of CEO Huang (n85).
Money moved out of the defensive sectors that led the past month (XLV +10.5%, XLP +7.6% over 1M) back into tech (n57). It looks more like re-positioning than a change in the outlook.
Thursday decides it: AMAT and Cisco after the close, NBIS before the open. Nvidia reports 17 Nov. The Anthropic IPO roadshow (n27) also adds a large new supply of AI stock for investors to absorb.

That reversed part of the roughly 21% slide since the start of November. The physical supply picture is getting looser: Saudi Arabia is back at 10.563M bpd, OPEC output rose about 2M bpd, and API showed a 9M-barrel build. Headlines keep pulling the price both ways.

Risk premium: 37 ships attacked in October, the most since the war began. LSEG says Hormuz flows would recover slowly even with a deal. Ukraine's drone strike hit Ust-Luga (n117).
Forecasts are far apart: the EIA sees about $100 for the rest of the year (n147), Jefferies $82.5 average for 2027 (n134), BNP $78 in early 2027 (n160).
BNO $59.33 (+1.66%) is down 8.9% over a month. Diesel is the tightest product, with heating oil +4.1% today.

brief.instructor_take: Here's how I read today. The equity bounce has one cause: CoreWeave showed that AI customers are still spending. Interest rates didn't help at all. The rate backdrop got worse overnight: a December hike is close to certain, 50bp is now being discussed, and the dollar is at a 19-month high. When stocks rise against rising yields, the gains are usually narrow and easy to reverse, and today fits. The Dow is flat and defensive sectors are lower, so this is money moving back into beaten-down tech, not a broad improvement. What less experienced investors miss is that this is a day with no cash bond market. The Treasury market reopens Thursday with claims, four Fed speakers, AMAT and Cisco, then PPI on Friday. The bond market hasn't reacted to today's equity rally yet. Second, watch what crypto is doing: it barely bounced while chips rose 6%. When an asset can't rally on a risk-on day, the selling hasn't finished, and the strong dollar is a direct headwind. My positioning: don't chase, let Thursday and Friday's events make the decisions, keep spare cash in SGOV earning around 4.1%, and only fill orders at levels I set in advance. Where I could be wrong: if PPI comes in soft and AMAT guides up, this rebound broadens, and I'll be buying back semis from higher prices. I accept that cost to avoid holding through two binary events.

top_ideas.title: Keep trimming a third of ETH into strength
top_ideas.one_liner: Keep ETH sells at $2,150/$2,200; exit below a $2,000 close
top_ideas.thesis: ETH is the weakest major layer-1 in a market that is losing liquidity. It is down 14% on the week, ETF demand is still negative, the dollar is at a 19-month high and the Fed is hiking. Bounces like today's +2.9% are where you sell, not where you buy.
top_ideas.reasoning: The evidence starts with the macro backdrop. Hot core CPI made a December hike close to certain and pushed the dollar to a 19-month high, and rising real yields hurt assets that pay no income. Next is demand. BTC ETFs have had four straight days of outflows, and ETH ETF selling slowed to -$1.3M but has not turned into buying. The overhang I take most seriously is JPMorgan's estimate of up to $2.8B in Strategy-related forced selling, which would hit the whole crypto complex. I'm applying relative strength: on a day when chips rose 6%, ETH rose under 3%, so the buyers aren't there yet. I trim ETH rather than BTC because ETH falls further when BTC falls (-17.9% vs -10.2% over the month), and its drawdown is deeper. I use limit orders 3–6% above the market because in a downtrend you get better exits by waiting for bounces than by selling into weakness. The $2,000 backstop is there in case the bounce never comes. I'll change my mind if ETH closes above $2,400 with three straight days of ETF inflows, which would mean demand has really turned.

top_ideas.sizing: One-third of the existing ETH position. No new crypto buying.

top_ideas.title: Don't chase the semis pop before AMAT
top_ideas.one_liner: Don't chase SMH's 6% pop; let AMAT decide on Thursday
top_ideas.thesis: SMH jumped 6.2% to $513.78 on CoreWeave's read-through, a day before AMAT reports and six days before Nvidia. Buying now takes on two binary events without any discount for that risk. I keep the trimmed weight and let AMAT's guidance trigger the re-entry.
top_ideas.reasoning: I'll be honest: yesterday's 'avoid' cost me the +6% bounce, and it's tempting to switch sides now. But look at what changed. CoreWeave beat on revenue, raised its guide and showed a $132.5B backlog, so the people buying AI computing power are still spending. That is real news about demand. It says nothing yet about equipment orders, which is what AMAT reports Thursday against a bar of about $4.05 EPS on $10.30B. Nvidia was downgraded this week and faces questions about its CEO before reporting on the 17th. The concept is event risk around a binary outcome: when a stock rises sharply just before a catalyst, good news is partly priced in and bad news hasn't been priced at all. Meanwhile a 10-year near 5% and a hiking Fed reduce what investors will pay today for future earnings, which hits long-duration growth stocks like semis hardest. I'm not calling the top. I just want AMAT's guidance to confirm the bounce before I put money in. If AMAT beats and raises and SMH holds above $508 into Friday's close, I was too cautious and I start rebuilding.

top_ideas.entry: No buying at $513. If AMAT beats and guides above consensus and SMH closes Fri 13 Nov above ~$508, buy half of the trimmed amount at the Mon 16 Nov open. Buy the second half only after Nvidia reports on 17 Nov and SMH holds above $508. If AMAT misses or guides below consensus, stay out until after Nvidia.
top_ideas.invalidation: AMAT beats and raises, and SMH holds above ~$508 through Nvidia's report on 17 Nov. At that point the avoid is over and I rebuild the full trimmed position.
top_ideas.sizing: Hold semis and tech at the trimmed weight. The re-entry tranche is half of the trimmed amount (roughly 1–2% of the portfolio), with the rest after Nvidia.

top_ideas.title: Finish the IEF ladder only at the $90.60 limit
top_ideas.one_liner: IEF second tranche only at $90.60; cancel if core PPI ≥0.5%
top_ideas.thesis: Fed hikes push up short-term yields most and tend to keep a lid on long-term ones. That leaves the 10-year near 5% as a good yield to lock in for a few months, and it protects the portfolio if the AI rebound fails. The first half is filled at $91.20. The second half waits at $90.60 through Friday's PPI, with a hard cancel rule.
top_ideas.reasoning: The CPI-day move is the evidence: the 2-year rose 17bp and the 10-year 10bp. That is a bear flattener, meaning the market is pricing hikes at the front of the curve rather than a permanent rise in long-term inflation. When the Fed tightens, long-term yields usually rise less because the hikes are expected to slow growth later. IEF at ~5% earns its yield while I wait and should rise if Thursday's AI earnings or Friday's PPI shake the equity rally, which is why I hold it rather than more stocks. I chose IEF over TLT because the 30-year at 5.36% carries more risk of investors demanding extra yield for holding long debt, and I don't need that much rate sensitivity. Conviction is lower than on the other two ideas. Waller is openly discussing 50bp, the dollar is at a 19-month high, and today's yield prints come from a closed cash market, so real price discovery returns Thursday. The first tranche is only about 0.35% underwater, which is small compared with the yield. I'll know I'm wrong if core PPI comes in at 0.5% or higher, if the 10-year closes above 5.20%, or if futures price 50bp in December as more likely than not. Any of those means the hiking cycle is steeper than one gradual 25bp step.

The re-entry rule hasn't triggered because it requires an AMAT beat-and-raise, and AMAT reports Thursday after the close. SMH is now above the $508 level ahead of the event, which raises the bar, not lowers it. Keep, with the re-entry clarified (Friday close above $508 after an AMAT beat, half Monday, half after Nvidia). 2) BUY IEF: the first half was filled at $91.20, and IEF is $90.88 (-0.35% before yield earned). The $90.60 second-half limit has not filled as far as I can tell (I don't have today's intraday low). The rationale still holds and nothing has invalidated it: the 10-year is about 5.00%, below 5.20%, and 50bp is not yet the base case. Keep through Friday, with conviction lowered to low because the Fed talk has turned more hawkish. 3) TRIM ETH: ETH is $2,080, so the $2,150/$2,200 sells are unfilled. Yesterday's implied level (about $2,020) stayed above the $2,000 backstop, so no sale was forced. The rationale has strengthened (dollar at a 19-month high, continued ETF outflows, Strategy forced-selling risk). Keep unchanged.

lesson.explanation: A bear flattener is when yields rise across the curve (bear) but short-term yields rise more than long-term ones (flattener). It is what a hiking cycle usually looks like. Two-year yields track the next few Fed moves closely. Ten-year yields also price the slower growth and lower inflation those hikes are expected to cause later. That's why short-dated bonds and cash reprice upward fast, and the 10-year often holds up relatively well once hikes are underway.
lesson.todays_example: On the official curve for 10 Nov, the 1-year rose 18bp and the 2-year 17bp, but the 10-year rose only 10bp and the 30-year 9bp. The 2s10s spread fell to +25bp. It's the reason I keep SGOV/bills for spare cash (bill yields are rising with each hike bet) while adding IEF only at a pre-set level near 5%.
